body_markdown:
### The pressure on utilities is real and growing


Security, DERs and smart grid assets are all pushing capex up, and every one of them needs coordination across stakeholders on capital programs. These aren’t separate projects running in parallel. They draw on the same sites, the same crews and the same budgets, and they have to be planned together.


### Private LTE adoption is uneven


Some utilities have finished their rollout. Many haven’t started, and others are testing the water with small local pilots. The range of progress in the room was wide, and so was the range of questions. For more on this area, see our page on[Private LTE for Utilities](https://sitenna.com/solution/private-lte-for-utilities/) .


### The case for owning your network is strong


Southern Linc’s account of its response to Hurricane Helene was a highlight of the week. Its “Barnyard” fleet of restoration kit, every piece named after a farmyard animal, got customers back online far faster than other carriers managed. For anyone weighing up the value of an owned network, it was a concrete example of what that control is worth when conditions are at their worst.


### The use cases keep multiplying


Connected devices, smart workforce tools, gas leak sensors, pole tilt sensors, weather stations, NB-IoT water meters, and plenty more. Every new use case adds assets to deploy, track and maintain, and more sites and contractors to coordinate.


### The hallway talk


The conversation all week was SpaceX’s deal for Grain Management’s 800 MHz spectrum, and what it means for owned network plans across utilities and the wider ecosystem. Nobody had a settled answer, but everyone had a view.


The Sitenna Team at the UBBA conference in Fort Worth


### Where the ambition meets the old way of running projects


Taken together, these are significant changes to how utilities operate, and large capital programs are starting, or already under way, to meet them. But that ambition often runs into the old way of running projects.


Hundreds of sites, towers, substations and fiber routes, with contractors on everyone. Disconnected tools. Spreadsheets one person owns and nobody else can see. Data that doesn’t match between teams. Uncertainty about whether a site is live, and sometimes about exactly where it is. When a program director asks for a status update, it can take hours to pull together, and it’s out of date by the time it lands.


### What holds teams back is the transition


Teams know this needs to change. What holds them back is the transition itself. How much work is involved? Will it disrupt live operations? Does it have to be a big-bang rollout, or can we pilot first? How long until we see value?


We hear these questions from utilities almost every day, and they’re fair ones.


Daniel Campion hosting the Tuesday Tech Talk, with Tim Valin of West Monroe and Paul Schmidt of Automation Exchange


### What we’ve seen work


Get a full baseline set up in weeks, not months. Give everyone, contractors included, one shared and validated view of every asset. Make reporting instant. And start small if you want to.


Adding headcount won’t fix overruns and cost leakage. One shared record of the program goes a lot further, and what we heard in Fort Worth backed that up.
